item.title: Dolly Parton's Imagination Library (232 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://imaginationlibrary.com/, See on Hacker News

Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library is dedicated to inspiring a love of reading by gifting books free of charge to children from birth to age five, through funding shared by Dolly Parton and local community partners in the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia and Republic of Ireland.

Inspired by her father’s inability to read and write Dolly started her Imagination Library in 1995 for the children within her home county. Today, her program spans five countries and gifts millions of free books each month to children around the world.

“When I was growing up in the hills of East Tennessee, I knew my dreams would come true. I know there are children in your community with their own dreams. They dream of becoming a doctor or an inventor or a minister. Who knows, maybe there is a little girl whose dream is to be a writer and singer.

The seeds of these dreams are often found in books and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world.”

In 1995, Dolly Parton launched an exciting new effort, Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, to benefit the children of her home county in East Tennessee, USA. Dolly’s vision was to foster a love of reading among her county’s preschool children and their families by providing them with the gift of a specially selected book each month.

By mailing high quality, age-appropriate books directly to their homes, she wanted children to be excited about books and to feel the magic that books can create. Moreover, she could ensure that every child would have books, regardless of their family’s income

item.title: Oregon Police Are Charging a Local News Outlet $2.5M for Records About One Cop (255 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://theintercept.com/2026/10/01/oregon-police-misconduct-public-records-cost-fee/, See on Hacker News

Lauren Harper is Freedom of the Press Foundation’s first Daniel Ellsberg Chair on Government Secrecy.

How much does it cost to get more information about a cop who punched someone in the face?

If you guessed anything lower than $2.5 million, you’d be wrong — at least according to the city of Eugene, Oregon.

In August, the local news outlet Double Sided Media filed a public records request for records about police officer Justin Peckels, which focused on potential misconduct between 2018 and 2026. Peckels has been the subject of community complaints, including for punching a resident in the face during a traffic stop, making the records vital for oversight and their release clearly in the public interest.

The city’s response is beyond belief. In its response to the request on Monday, the Eugene Police Department claimed searching for records and processing the request would take at least 44,816 hours of staff time and cost approximately $2,484,599.04. (A separate request by the outlet for similar records concerning a former police officer, Eric Klinko, was met with a comparatively modest estimate of $195,869.52, for a grand total of nearly $2.7 million for both requests.)

“Once the City receives payment of $2,484,599.04 staff will continue processing your request,” the letter from the department’s public records division read. “If the actual cost of processing your request exceeds the amount you have paid the City, you will be required to pay the difference before the City will provide the records you have requested.”

Peckels’s file is either the largest in the world, or city officials have intentionally maintained their databases in such a way as to ensure fulfilling public records requests is prohibitively expensive. The city’s response points, at a minimum, to the latter. It justified the multimillion-dollar price tag by claiming it couldn’t narrow the custodians whose records it would need to search, despite the targeted nature of the request, and maintained it must search all records of all city employees, past and present.

By that logic, if someone ever worked in Eugene’s parks and recreation department, their records could contain responsive information about police misconduct, and must be manually pulled and reviewed, one by one.

This goes far beyond incompetence. It’s an intentional effort to make a response artificially voluminous — and cost prohibitive — to intimidate the journalist into dropping it entirely. 

Normally, agencies are required to search the specific custodians most likely to possess responsive records, not every groundskeeper or clerk on the city payroll. If the city were acting in good faith, officials would have asked Double Sided Media to help them identify the most likely record-holders, not take it upon themselves to cast a citywide dragnet as its first step.

What makes Eugene’s money-grab particularly galling is its technology double standard. While it apparently can’t invest in efficient search software, the police department recently signed a two-year $342,000 contract for nearly 60 AI-powered Flock automated license plate readers. This project was so secretive that the ACLU of Oregon had to sue the city for records about how the cameras were being used and demonstrates, among other inclinations, the city’s eagerness to employ sophisticated software to deploy against residents. 

Yet that technological sophistication disappears as soon as a journalist requests public records about the department’s internal accountability process, and simple keyword searches are suddenly cumbersome. 

Troublingly, Eugene’s $2.5 million bill is not an anomaly.

In 2015, the Department of Defense told a Freedom of Information Act requester, who was asking for records on tools used to preserve data on seized devices, that fulfilling their request would take 15 million hours and cost $660 million.

The same year, the Drug Enforcement Administration told a requester it would cost $1.46 million for records about the DEA’s role in the search and capture of the Mexican cartel boss Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzman.

In 2019, the Army tried to charge $300,000 to release military base water test results for the presence of toxic chemicals. The Army agreed to waive the exorbitant fee after facing intense backlash. 

The list goes on and on.

Luckily, records requesters seeking federal documents have a defense against these capricious invoices. Recent FOIA amendments aim to ensure if an agency misses its response deadlines, it can’t charge most fees. 

At the local level, however, these protections disintegrate. While Oregon grants agencies the discretion to reduce fees when the disclosure would benefit the public, agencies routinely ignore these provisions.

For small newsrooms like Double Sided Media, a $2.5 million invoice is effectively a gag order that was never actually about covering costs, but bullying the requester to drop their inquiry (all while Eugene Police Department launches its own “press” initiative to document its policing). It also sets the precedent for using this chilling tactic on any journalist or watchdog as it sees fit. 

Double Sided Media is rightly appealing the fee estimate, and it should prevail. But cities like Eugene will continue these efforts unless lawmakers across the country force agencies to adopt fee caps, mandate public-interest fee waivers for journalists, and require agencies to procure software that allows them to respond to records requests in an efficient and timely manner.

Until then, police departments will likely continue to issue multimillion-dollar ransoms for their records — weaponizing the public’s right to know into another avenue for police to operate with impunity.

item.title: I refuse to accept a censored Internet. Join Me at FOSDEM 27 (284 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://talkweb.eu/openweb/4558/, See on Hacker News

As one of the managers of the Digital Dissident Devroom, I invite you to be part of a conversation we cannot afford to ignore.

Around the world, people are being silenced, monitored, and denied access to information. Free software can help change that, but only if we build it together. We need tools people can trust and control to communicate safely, expose the truth, and resist censorship.

This devroom brings together developers, researchers, activists, and everyone committed to digital freedom. We want real solutions, honest lessons, and collaboration across projects, not product pitches.

If you believe technology should serve people, not control them, join us. Bring your ideas, experience, and questions. Let’s build the tools that help keep freedom alive.

Our focus complements other devrooms, including Decentralized Internet and Privacy, which explores the broader decentralized ecosystem. While they focus on technologies, we focus on the people under threat and the complete chain of tools that can protect them.

How to apply to speak at the dev room?

  1. Go to FOSDEM’s official CFP portal from here and login or register.
  2. Click on “Submit a proposal”
  3. Then fill in the form and select “Digital Dissident” as a track.
  4. Done!
  5. Please note that by doing this you also accept the FOSDEM Code of Conduct.

Define: Digital Dissident Developer Room

Privacy and anonymity tools each have a home at FOSDEM: the network, security, decentralised and messaging rooms, and various main-track and lightning talks. Someone living under an authoritarian regime (Russia, Iran, China, Belarus, Myanmar and others) never uses a single tool, though. Their day-to-day security depends on a chain of tools that has to hold up end to end:

  1. reaching the network at all (censorship circumvention),
  2. communicating without leaking metadata,
  3. collecting, verifying and storing evidence safely,
  4. publishing or leaking it without exposing the author,
  5. doing all this on devices and infrastructure that are themselves a risk.

The weakest link decides the outcome. Talks about one tool rarely cover how it fits with the others, where the seams are, or what breaks at the hand-offs (for example, a circumvention transport that is fingerprinted, or a messenger whose push notifications tie your identity to a Google or Apple account). Nobody currently owns that cross-project view.

What this devroom does. It brings developers of circumvention, anonymity, messaging, publishing and whistleblowing tools into one room. It is deliberately not about any single project. Each session is judged on how well it advances the toolchain: interoperability, shared threat models, shared failure data, and shared engineering practice.

Why now. Censorship in Russia, Iran and China has grown much more sophisticated. It now includes national allow-lists and whitelist-only internet shutdowns, TLS and QUIC fingerprinting, deep packet inspection with active probing, throttling of specific protocols, mobile internet shutdowns, app-store removal of circumvention tools, and mandatory state-run messengers and “sovereign internet” routing. Anti-censorship developers have responded with pluggable transports, domain fronting alternatives, mixnets, decentralised and email-based messaging, and new obfuscation protocols. Progress is fast but fragmented. At FOSDEM 2026 the relevant talks were scattered: Vitaly Repin’s “The Russian Censorship Circumvention, Tom’s Traps, and Jerry’s VPN: A 5-Year Journey” (Saturday, H.1302, Network track) drew a large audience, while NymVPN and Delta Chat’s multi-relay messaging (both Sunday, Decentralized Internet and Privacy devroom) and other related talks ran in other rooms. A single devroom lets that audience and those speakers meet in one place.

Relationship to the existing “Decentralized Internet and Privacy” devroom. That room covers decentralised technology broadly (P2P protocols, browsers, code collaboration, key infrastructure), and censorship or anonymity is only a part of it. Digital Dissident is different: the organising principle is a user under threat and the end-to-end chain that protects them, not a technology class. We want to work with, not against, that room, and will coordinate schedules so the two don’t overlap, and will point overflow speakers to whichever room fits.

Themes (details in the CfP below):

  • Censorship circumvention and transport: obfuscation, fingerprint resistance, active-probing defence, bridge distribution, resilience to protocol whitelisting and full shutdowns.
  • Metadata-resistant communication: mixnets, onion routing, decentralised and federated messengers, store-and-forward and offline-first (mesh, sneakernet, Bluetooth/Wi-Fi Direct).
  • Secure reporting and publishing: whistleblowing platforms, source protection, document sanitisation, provenance and authenticity, censorship-resistant hosting.
  • Devices and operational security: hardened mobile and desktop systems, amnesic systems, seizure and border-crossing scenarios, forensic resistance.
  • Usability and threat modelling for at-risk users: onboarding under duress, safe defaults, training, measuring what really works in the field.
  • Measurement and adversary analysis: how censors detect and block, open data on blocking events, reproducible censorship research.
  • Digital sovereignty from Big Tech (secondary theme): reducing dependence on centralised platforms, app stores, push infrastructure, cloud and identity providers, both for individuals and for civil-society organisations.

Structure. A mix of formats to keep a full room engaged across the whole session:

  • 20 to 30 minute technical talks
  • A closing open discussion on interoperability gaps and shared next steps

Programme quality. Organisers will review all submissions on technical merit and fit to the toolchain framing, and will aim for a balance of projects, regions and speakers (established projects, new projects, researchers, people from affected communities). Every talk should include an explicit threat model and an honest account of limitations.

Projects and communities we intend to invite (no commitments yet): Nym (mixnet), Delta Chat / chatmail, SimpleX, the Fediverse (ActivityPub implementations and instance operators), Nostr, Psiphon and other circumvention and VPN providers, plus Tor-ecosystem, Reticulum and mesh-networking projects, whistleblowing and secure-submission platforms, and censorship-measurement researchers. Several of these projects presented at FOSDEM 2026.

Code of Conduct. We will follow the FOSDEM Code of Conduct. In addition, talks that describe circumvention or anonymity should avoid operational details that would endanger specific users in the field.

Important Dates

  • Sat, 24 October 2026: Call for Participation opens
  • Mon, 30 November 2026, 23:59 UTC: Call for Participation ends
  • Wed, 2 December 2026: Speakers notified
  • Fri, 4 December 2026: Deadline for speakers to confirm
  • Mon, 7 December 2026: Schedule published
  • The twenty-sixth edition of FOSDEM will take place on Saturday 30th and Sunday 31st January 2027 at the usual location, ULB Campus Solbosch in Brussels.

item.title: A 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs for skin cancer diagnosis (306 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://lynchlab.net/llm-skin-cancer, See on Hacker News

I am a dermatologist. I tested the ability of GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 to diagnosis skin cancer and found that they were less accurate than I expected. I compared to a 10-year old CNN and to my surprise found that this was superior.

This is a melanoma.

I showed these two images - a clinical photograph and a dermoscopic (skin microscope) image - to GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, two of the most capable AI models available in October 2026. Both said it was a seborrhoeic keratosis, a harmless warty growth, and that the patient could be discharged. I then showed them to fine-tuned version of Inception v3, a convolutional neural network (CNN) first published by Google in 2015 and fine-tuned here on public dermatology images. The CNN got the right answer based on the dermoscopy view.

It was one of 200 biopsy-proven lesions I gave to all three. The CNN named the right diagnosis (out of 6 possiblities) for 125 of them (62%). The two frontier LLMs named it for 84 and 85 (42%). A ten-year-old network, fine-tuned for about twenty minutes, beat both of them at recognising skin cancer.

The test#

The lesions come from MILK10k, a public dataset released through the International Skin Imaging Collaboration in 2025, in which each lesion is photographed twice: a clinical close-up and a dermoscopic image taken through the illuminated magnifying lens dermatologists use. I drew 200 lesions at random, all confirmed by histopathology:

  • 100 that should not be discharged: 30 melanomas, 25 basal cell carcinomas, 25 squamous cell carcinomas (including Bowen’s disease) and 20 actinic keratoses.
  • 100 that are safe to discharge: 50 benign naevi (moles) and 50 seborrhoeic keratoses.

Every lesion was biopsied, including the benign ones, so these are harder to diagnose: a mole that somebody decided to cut out is one that worried a clinician.

The LLMs were given both images and nothing else, and asked, as a clinician might use them, for the most likely of the six diagnoses (or “unsure”), a confidence, a second choice, and whether the lesion could be safely discharged with no treatment, biopsy or follow-up. Both models got the same prompt at default settings, and neither refused a case.

The CNN is deliberately not state of the art. I used Inception v3 pretrained on everyday photographs and then fine-tuned all layers on 68,011 dermoscopic and clinical images from the ISIC Archive on a single H100 GPU. These 200 test lesions, and every other photograph of the same lesion or patient, were removed from its data (including the validation set) before training, so it had never seen them, and they were not used to choose the model or set its threshold. It scored both images of each lesion, combined them with most of the weight on the dermoscopic image, and chose from the same six diagnoses.

You can try the CNN yourself. Remarkably the model is small enough to run entirely in a phone browser using WebGPU. Nothing is uploaded, and its random sample button draws from these same 200 lesions.

Diagnosis: 62% against 42%#

The CNN was right more often overall and on most diagnoses. Allowing a second choice, it reached 173 of 200 against 134 and 138. It named 13 of the 30 melanomas against 8 and 11. The biggest gap was on the harmless lesions: it recognised 37 of 50 moles and 26 of 50 seborrhoeic keratoses, against 16 and 13 for GPT-6 Astra and 33 and 6 for Claude Fable 5.1. It was one short of GPT-6 Astra on basal cell carcinoma and behind both LLMs on actinic keratosis.

The models also failed differently. Each LLM had a favourite answer: GPT-6 Astra called 75 lesions basal cell carcinoma when 25 were, including 14 of the 30 melanomas, and Claude Fable 5.1 called 53 lesions actinic keratosis when 20 were. The CNN’s errors on melanoma went the other way: of the 17 it got wrong, it called 8 a naevus and 6 a seborrhoeic keratosis.

The results in one table#

GPT-6 Astra Claude Fable 5.1 CNN (Inception v3)
Correct diagnosis (of 200) 84 (42%) 85 (42%) 125 (62%)
Correct in first or second choice 134 138 173
Melanoma as first choice (of 30) 8 11 13
Unsafe lesions kept (of 100) 97 96 77 at its preset threshold; 98 or 99 when matched
Safe lesions discharged (of 100) 32 22 76 at its preset threshold
Melanomas discharged (of 30) 3 4 18 at its preset threshold; 2 or 1 when matched

Caveats#

  • Small numbers. Two hundred lesions are enough to show the pattern but not to rank close results, and 30 melanomas give wide uncertainty on the figure that matters most. Each LLM case was run once; answers vary between runs.
  • Hard cases. Every lesion was biopsied. On ordinary images from the archive the CNN separated lesions that should and should not be discharged far better (area under the ROC curve 0.96, against 0.86 here).
  • Contamination. MILK10k has been public since 2025, so the LLMs could have seen it in training; if anything that would have helped them. The CNN certainly had not.
  • Not state of the art. Inception v3 is a baseline. State of the art skin cancer diagnosis AI uses ensembles of images transformers trained on more data, and the regulated products built on them perform considerably better.

Asked as a patient#

Asked as a patient instead, with the clinical photograph alone and the question “do I need to see a doctor?”, both LLMs advised seeing a doctor in almost every case, harmless lesions included: for 99 and 98 of a further 100 biopsy-proven melanomas.

Conclusion#

A small, old, specialised network using an outdated architecture recognises skin lesions far better than two frontier LLMs.

Run it yourself#

The cases, prompts, every LLM reply and the scoring code are in one download, and the CNN is here.

I designed the test and made the clinical rulings. The analysis and the first drafts were produced with Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding tool, which runs on a Claude model; one of the two LLMs tested is also Anthropic’s. Scoring was done by script against the histology.

Images are from the MILK10k dataset (MILK study team, International Skin Imaging Collaboration), used under a CC BY-NC licence.

Dr Magnus Lynch is a Consultant Dermatologist and Mohs Surgeon at Guy's Hospital and Honorary Reader (equivalent of Associate Professor) at King's College London. His clinical work covers skin cancer, Mohs and facial reconstructive surgery, and lasers; his research covers the cell biology of skin cancers and scars and the use of AI in dermatology. Full profile.

item.title: AI use leads UC Berkeley math professor to see 'no point' in grading homework (154 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.dailycal.org/news/campus/academics/ai-use-leads-uc-berkeley-math-professor-to-see-no-point-in-grading-homework/article_bdf1eae2-c08b-491f-b9f1-81a7cea177de.html, See on Hacker News

Richard Borcherds, a UC Berkeley professor and Fields medalist, no longer grades his students’ homework. 

After seeing how many of his students used AI to consistently receive top scores, he felt there was “no point” in paying readers to grade for correctness in homework, as AI use is now unavoidable. 

Borcherds revealed this in a sit-down interview Tuesday, following OpenAI’s announcement that AI agents apparently solved one of mathematics’ most difficult unsolved problems, the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem.

“If AI continues to improve at present rate, then, in a few years, there’ll be nothing human mathematicians can do that AI can’t do better,” Borcherds said. 

Borcherds said he currently grades on completion if a student hands in their homework. He admitted that it is “not a very good system,” but at the moment, he has no alternative.

Borcherds stated he no longer knows whether to encourage students to go into the math department, as it seemed five years ago that being a mathematician was one of the safest careers from the AI boom.

“I have no idea what to advise. I even asked ChatGPT this exact question, and even ChatGPT said it didn’t have any idea what was going to happen,” Borcherds said. 

He described a plentiful amount of “inertia” in the academic system and said he wouldn’t be surprised if things stayed the same in the math department for a couple years despite AI developments. 

He drew a comparison to physical paper journals, which publish even though they have been “utterly pointless” for two decades. 

“There have been plenty of technical breakthroughs in the past — hand weaving was put out of business by looms, and horses were put out of business by motor cars, and so on,” Borcherds said. “This is the first time anything like this has happened in mathematics, though.”

The Berkeley Division of the Academic Senate asks that faculty include a statement about course expectations including the use of AI tools for coursework in course syllabi, according to an email from Anne Marie Richard, assistant vice provost for undergraduate education and chief academic technology officer. However, she said the direct policies on AI use can vary dramatically with course level and focus area. 

Campus has tried several AI detection tools, including Turnitin and Rumi, but have determined that these tools aren’t adequate enough to be standardized on campus.

AI policy for classes is up to the discretion of faculty, but there is a growing database of sample AI use statements available in the AI Hub, the campus directory for AI tools, training and policies, for faculty to use in their syllabi, according to Richard.

item.title: JetBrains Thinkrail (114 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/JetBrains/thinkrail, See on Hacker News

ThinkRail is the agentic IDE that gets better every time you use it — learning your project through living specs today, and building its own capabilities tomorrow.

We built a rich interface around the pi coding agent, isolated work into separate workspaces, and gave the agent durable project knowledge through living specs and reusable skills. Next, we're adding full extension support, so ThinkRail can create the tools it needs based on how you actually work.

Website: thinkrail.ai · Blog: thinkrail.ai/blog

⭐ If you find ThinkRail useful, give it a star — it helps others discover it.

A pi session and the change it made, scoped to an isolated git-worktree workspace.

What you get

  • Isolated workspaces. Open any git repo as a project and cut workspaces from it as git worktrees, each with its own branch and working directory. Agents work in parallel without touching your checkout; merge the good branch, delete the rest. You can also attach existing worktrees or explicitly work in the project folder itself. Finished and dormant workspaces settle onto a per-project shelf on their own — when their pull request merges or closes, or after a quiet week — and come back the moment you work in them. The topbar shows where the active branch stands against origin and its pull request, with the next step one click away: publish, push, or open a PR described from the plan, the commits, your PR template, or an agent-written draft. Once a GitHub PR is open it shows the CI checks and review decision, and lets you mark it ready, hand failing checks or a diverged branch to the agent, merge it with the repository's last-used method, reopen it, or delete the remote branch.
  • A real IDE around the agent. A splittable workbench of Monaco editor tabs, a Files tree with live git change marks and a Changed view, terminals, and documents — all scoped to the active workspace. Leave anchored review comments on files and diffs and send them to a chat as structured context, or open the worktree in your installed IDE.
  • Chats that stream like the engine thinks. Several concurrent pi sessions per workspace, each with its own model and live token and cost readout. Steer a running turn or queue a follow-up, delegate to subagents, and work a shared plan the agent updates and you edit — each completed step can be committed and reviewed on its own.
  • Specs as ground truth. A connected graph of SPEC.md files lives beside the code; the agent reads, searches, and maintains it through dedicated spec_* tools, so intent survives the session. The read-only Specs tool renders the graph as a tree in the workbench.
  • Skills and workflows. Portable Agent Skills you already keep for other coding agents are read in place, and bundled workflows guide project setup, design brainstorming, and shipping a pull request — pushing the workspace branch and opening or updating its GitHub PR through your own gh.
  • Agent tools beyond the shell. Web research, and inline diagrams, option comparisons and file previews rendered right in the chat — when the agent proposes a UI change it shows a before/after mockup you can comment on like a diff. Settings → Extensions lists the ThinkRail extensions the agent gets and lets you switch each one off.
  • MCP servers. Connect the MCP servers in your pi mcp.json (or add them, and a few presets, from Settings): ThinkRail asks in the chat before calls the server does not mark read-only (or always allows the tools you trust in a project), keeps servers a repository defines off until you approve them, signs you in to OAuth servers from Settings, and shows each chat's servers next to its background commands and subagents.
  • Your providers, your credentials. Sign in with JetBrains AI or connect any provider through pi's own auth. ThinkRail has no accounts of its own.
  • Desktop app or browser. A native desktop app, or the thinkrail CLI that opens the same app in your browser. Both embed the same engine host; app state lives under ~/.thinkrail.
  • Your language. Settings → Language follows your system language or a language you pick; English and Simplified Chinese are built in. Add a language ThinkRail doesn't ship yet by dropping a translated en.json into ~/.thinkrail/locales — it applies as you save. Agent replies and tool output stay as the agent wrote them.

The project's spec graph as a tree, with the spec itself rendered alongside.

Install

ThinkRail ships in two additive forms: a native desktop installer and the self-contained thinkrail CLI. Both are published with SHA256SUMS on the releases page.

Desktop

Download the thinkrail-desktop-* asset for your platform:

  • macOS (Apple Silicon) — open the DMG. There is no Intel desktop build.

  • Windows x64 — extract the complete setup ZIP, then run its setup executable in place, next to its payload.

  • Linux x64 / ARM64 — extract the setup tarball and run installer. Desktop builds need glibc 2.38+ with GTK 3, WebKitGTK 4.1, Ayatana AppIndicator 3, and librsvg 2 — Ubuntu 24.04 or newer:

    sudo apt install libgtk-3-0 libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0 libayatana-appindicator3-1 librsvg2-2

Packaged stable and nightly desktop builds check for updates in the background and offer them in Settings → Updates: Download → Preparing update → Install & Restart. Nothing is applied until you choose Install & Restart. ThinkRail then shows the installation's progress and log, closes, and reopens on the new version. After the restart it tells you whether the update installed. If it didn't, it explains why and offers to retry. The updater appears only when the package carries a valid HTTPS feed identity; installations that predate that identity need one manual installation first.

Command line

The installer downloads the right binary, verifies its SHA-256 checksum, and puts thinkrail on your PATH.

macOS / Linux (also Windows under Git Bash):

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash

Windows — the same command works from cmd and PowerShell:

powershell -c "irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.ps1 | iex"

Then run thinkrail, optionally with a git repo to open as a project:

thinkrail needs git on your PATH and a model provider — sign in with JetBrains AI from the app or use your own provider credentials. thinkrail --help lists the flags; thinkrail --version prints the build.

Nightly builds, pinned versions, updates, and uninstall

The installer takes --channel stable|nightly and --version; a pinned version must belong to the selected channel:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel stable --version 0.1.2
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly --version 0.2.0-nightly.10

On Windows the options are environment variables (THINKRAIL_CHANNEL, THINKRAIL_VERSION, THINKRAIL_PREFIX, THINKRAIL_NO_MODIFY_PATH):

$env:THINKRAIL_CHANNEL='nightly'; irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.ps1 | iex   # PowerShell
set "THINKRAIL_CHANNEL=stable" && set "THINKRAIL_VERSION=0.1.2" && powershell -c "irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.ps1 | iex"   # cmd

Installed stable and nightly CLI hosts periodically offer Run Update in Settings → Updates. It runs the host machine's thinkrail update in the background — also when the UI is open in a browser on another machine — and a successful update asks you to restart the host manually. You can run thinkrail update directly on any platform: it re-runs the installer for the installed channel and replaces <prefix>/bin/thinkrail[.exe]; pass --channel or --version only for an explicit override.

thinkrail uninstall removes the executable, the PATH entry the installer added, and the install metadata, and asks whether to delete your ~/.thinkrail app state (kept by default — --remove-data deletes it, -y skips the questions).

Prefer a manual install? Download a binary and SHA256SUMS from the releases page and verify the checksum. For self-update to work, rename it to thinkrail (thinkrail.exe on Windows) and place it at <prefix>/bin/thinkrail[.exe]; a binary kept under its release filename or elsewhere must be replaced manually or reinstalled with the script.

Platform notes

Platform Desktop CLI
macOS Apple Silicon DMG signed binary
macOS Intel no Electrobun build not prebuilt — build from source
Windows x64 signed setup executable and app binaries signed .exe
Linux x64 / ARM64 setup tarball, unsigned unsigned

JetBrains signs the Windows CLI, the desktop setup executable, and every executable and DLL the desktop app installs. The macOS CLI is signed but not yet notarized. Signed and notarized desktop DMGs require the coordinated JetBrains service pipeline; older published DMGs and locally built packages may still be unsigned and blocked by Gatekeeper. Linux artifacts are unsigned.

Analytics & privacy

ThinkRail collects basic usage events — launches, chat creation, message sends, provider connections — tied to a random installation ID. Usage analytics never include prompts, code, files, credentials, or account identity. Error reports are also always sent, tied to the same installation ID, so we can fix crashes: the error type and code and where in ThinkRail's own code it happened. They never include error messages, file paths, names, URLs, or anything from your projects or extensions. Additional product usage and how you found ThinkRail are shared only while Share additional usage data is on; the switch is offered at first launch and lives in Settings → Privacy. When launching from the command line, thinkrail --no-analytics (or THINKRAIL_NO_ANALYTICS=1) turns additional sharing off for that run. With additional sharing on, a packaged build may open the ThinkRail blog in your browser once to link your installation to the website visit that brought you here — only where you accepted marketing cookies on the website or no consent is required — and that link expires after 30 days.

Under the hood

ThinkRail is a thin host that runs pi in-process and bridges it to a rich web UI. pi owns models, skills, compaction, cost, and session state; the app owns the workspace, the editor, and the wire — it never assembles prompts behind your back. Three rings:

  • Engine host — packages/server (+ packages/shared): a Bun.serve HTTP+WS host with one in-process pi session per chat, launched by apps/cli or apps/desktop.
  • The wire — packages/contracts: the typed, versioned protocol between host and UI.
  • UI client — apps/web: React 19 + Zustand + Tailwind v4, shipped independently; it dials a host over the wire and depends on the contracts only.

goal-and-requirements.md and architecture.md are the canonical product and design specs. ThinkRail is developed spec-first: a SPEC.md sits beside every module, and a change that moves a boundary, contract, or decision updates the spec in the same change.

Developing ThinkRail

You need Bun 1.4.4 (the pinned package manager and runtime), Node.js ≥ 22.19 (required by the in-process pi engine), and an authenticated pi provider for agent work.

git clone https://github.com/JetBrains/thinkrail.git
cd thinkrail
bun install
bun run dev                          # host + web client together; Ctrl+C stops both
bun run --filter @thinkrail/cli dev  # browser launcher
bun run build:binary                 # standalone CLI artifact
bun run desktop:dev                  # package and open the Electrobun app
bun run desktop:build                # package without opening it

item.title: Tool book of a Nuremberg knight from 1505 (159 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://loeffelholz-codex.org/en/, See on Hacker News

In 1505, Martin Löffelholz, a Nuremberg patrician (i.e. a member of the city's ruling families) and knight, began to put together a book. Not a diary, not a family chronicle - a tool book. He drew what occupied his mind: drills with interchangeable blades. Threads and the tools to cut them. A workbench with a vise. A swivel chair on casters. A spiral staircase that can be swung out of the way. A crossbow, taken apart into its individual parts. A cradle whose rockers are filled with mercury.

Today the book is in Kraków. It has been fully digitized and is in the public domain - and yet in more than 500 years no one has ever read it in full. There is no transcription, no edition, no translation.

That is about to change.

The Codex has 154 pages. 127 of them have been reviewed, 27 not yet.

What You Will Find Here

Each of the 154 pages gets a page of its own. Depending on how far the work has come, it has:

  • the facsimile in the best available resolution, to zoom in on
  • a heading - what is actually shown here?
  • the transcription in the original spelling, with uncertain passages marked in color
  • a reading in modern English
  • a suggested interpretation: what the object is, how it works, why it is remarkable
  • What Stands Out Today - what strikes a person of the 21st century about this page as odd, astonishing or unexpectedly modern
  • open questions and questions for craftspeople, honestly labeled as such

Popular Topics

Six pages to start with

See all 154 pages →

How Reliable Is the Information on the Folio Pages?

As reliable as it says on each page - no more and no less.

Pages without a special note have been editorially reviewed: carefully checked and corrected. We go through every page thoroughly: we examine the original drawing, the published research as far as we can find it, the transcription and the AI's suggested explanation. The goal is to understand exactly what Löffelholz drew there - and how it might have worked. The engineering background of our project lead Dirk Schornstein comes in handy here. Then we rewrite the page so that it explains the picture and how the device works in steps that are as easy to follow as possible. If a function is uncertain or cannot be determined, the page says so.

Pages with the note “raw transcription” at the very top are a first draft. An AI produced the transcription and the interpretation. I have read these pages, but I have not yet checked and corrected them line by line.

Anything read with uncertainty is marked in color. Anything that could not be deciphered is left as a gap. Interpretations are explicitly suggestions.

Nothing is presented here as certain that is not. That is one of the most important rules of this project, and it has applied from the very beginning.

Who Is Doing This

I am Dirk Schornstein, a graduate engineer (Diplom-Ingenieur) and technology enthusiast. I discovered the Löffelholz Codex a few years ago, and it has fascinated me ever since.

I still have not found a place where truly every page of the Codex is described and interpreted in detail. I want to change that. But as a single person, I can only take on a project this big with AI as a tool. The AI does the groundwork - but every reviewed page carries a lot of me. My goal is to understand every single device in this book - and to explain it clearly to others. I can't do it all on my own - and I need your help.

More about me →

Löffelholz Mystery of the Month

Some pages of the Codex don't give up their secrets easily. Every month, I tackle one of those mysteries - and since October, we solve them together.

Open · Löffelholz Mystery October 2026

Mystery: The Dagger (17r)

A bow, a dagger, a pile of loose parts and a sheath. How many objects does this page really show?

All Löffelholz Mysteries →

Contribute

This project is too big for one person. We are looking for people who

  • can read Early New High German - or would like to learn
  • know a craft: woodworkers, smiths, wood turners, gunsmiths. What kind of tool is this? Does it work like that? What is missing from the drawing?
  • want to build replicas, even if it's just a compass
  • have expert knowledge of the history of technology, manuscripts, arms and armor, hunting

Anyone who helps correct a page will be named on that page. It is not much in return, but it is the most honest thing I can offer. Feedback is always welcome - positive or negative. This site should keep getting better.

How to contribute →

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Löffelholz Codex?

A house book from Nuremberg, begun in 1505 by Martin Löffelholz von Kolberg: 154 pages of tools, machines, locks, weapons, hunting gear and recipes, drawn and briefly captioned. The original is held by the Biblioteka Jagiellońska in Kraków. The Codex is described in detail on loeffelholz-codex.org under “What Is the Codex?”

What language is the Löffelholz Codex written in?

In Early New High German, in the written language of Nuremberg - so it is German, but the German of 1505, with no fixed spelling. The same word can be spelled two different ways on one page, a stroke over a letter stands for an n or m, and the words of the workshop are not in any modern dictionary. This is explained in detail, with examples from the manuscript, on loeffelholz-codex.org under “What Is the Codex?”

Where is the original Löffelholz Codex kept, and can it be viewed?

In the Biblioteka Jagiellońska in Kraków, under the shelfmark Ms. Berol. germ. quart. 132. The manuscript has been fully digitized and can be viewed freely in the digitized copy of the Jagiellonian Library at jbc.bj.uj.edu.pl. Where the book comes from and how it came to Kraków is explained on loeffelholz-codex.org in the Fact Sheet

Is there a complete transcription or translation of the Löffelholz Codex?

Not a published one that we know of. There is literature on individual pages and a detailed video discussion, but no edition that reads and interprets all 154 pages. That is exactly what loeffelholz-codex.org has been building since 2026, page by page: facsimile, transcription in the original spelling, a reading in modern English and a suggested interpretation, each page with its editing status clearly stated.

Who was Martin Löffelholz von Kolberg?

A Nuremberg patrician and knight who died in 1533, and the author of the Löffelholz Codex. For 28 years he was Pfleger (warden) of the fortress of Lichtenau, and between 1507 and 1509 he was held captive for more than a year - shackles and locks take up a strikingly large share of his book. His life is described in detail on loeffelholz-codex.org under “About Martin Löffelholz”

And Now Have Fun!

I hope you enjoy exploring and are amazed by what the people of Nuremberg already knew in the early 16th century: a drill with an interchangeable chuck, an office chair on casters, the fire striker, the carabiner and much more!

item.description:

Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years.
TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust.

A hot potato: It seems that the once-popular trend of entering AI-generated content in competitions made for humans hasn't gone away. The winner of one of the world's most prestigious scientific photography awards has just had his title stripped from him after his entry was determined to have been created using AI.

Nikon's 16th annual Small World in Motion contest is open to any movie or digital time-lapse photography taken through the microscope.

This year's winner was Dr. Ning Xu, from Tsinghua University in China, whose video captured tiny cilia beating in the airways of a child with primary ciliary dyskinesia, a rare respiratory disorder.

But Xu's entry raised several concerns among members of the scientific community. Some researchers said there were abnormalities in the structure and size of the cells and that their features appeared and disappeared in a way not seen in cellular biology.

One associate professor at the University of Florida said some of the structures "pop in and out of existence" and the cilia "appear from nowhere," which are classic indications that a video was AI-generated.

A more damning discovery came from PhD student Ian Donovan at UT Southwestern Medical Center, who said the source image appeared to contain a distinctive watermark indicating it had been AI-generated. Two former competition judges also raised concerns about the clip's legitimacy.

In a now-deleted LinkedIn post, Xu admitted to using AI in the video, but he said it was only used to "distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images from the super-resolution optical imaging" during post-processing.

He added that AI had not been used to generate the video itself, the cilia, or their movement.

Xu insists that he has not broken competition rules. While enhancing the visibility of microscopic structures is common and allowed, researchers typically use techniques such as applying stains and dyes to the samples themselves.

However, Xu's explanation doesn't account for the abnormalities found in his video. Some scientists said the doubts could have been removed if Xu had shared the RAW grayscale video.

An investigation by Nikon found that Xu had violated the competition's rules, and he was subsequently stripped of his prize. The top spot has instead been awarded to Nguyen Nam Nhat of Vietnam, who entered a video of a tiny roundworm and a single-celled organism.

Following the incident, Nikon said in a statement that it plans to "revisit rules and evaluation procedures for future competition entries."

We've seen several examples of AI-generated images being entered into, and sometimes winning, art competitions going back years. A Midjourney image won a category in Colorado State Fair's annual art competition in 2022, while another creation won a photography contest hosted by Australian photo retailer digiDirect in 2023.

There was also the case of an artist who won a category in the 2023 Sony World Photography Awards but refused his prize because his image (below) was AI-generated – something that seems quite obvious these days.

In a more satisfying story from 2024, a man who won a digital art competition using an AI-generated image and was thoroughly unapologetic about it complained that people had started stealing his "work" and he couldn't copyright it.

item.title: Meta Ignores Brazilian Court Order to End Bolsonaro Favoritism (462 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.panamericandispatch.org/p/meta-ignores-brazilian-court-order, See on Hacker News

by Otávio Rosso

Sleeping Giants Brasil and the organization CTRL+Z sent new evidence to the Superior Electoral Court on Monday. The groups say it points to possible unequal treatment by Meta of the campaigns of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, of the Workers’ Party, and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, of the Liberal Party.

The groups argue that Instagram and WhatsApp tools keep showing results that would favor the Liberal Party candidate. They also say the tools link Lula to derogatory content. This continues despite an electoral court order that Meta ensure equal conditions for both candidates.

Journalist Mônica Bergamo broke the story today in Folha de S.Paulo. According to her report, the organizations filed a petition addressed to Superior Electoral Court Justice Marco Aurélio Bellizze, who is overseeing the court caset. They asked him to order the alleged irregularities fixed within 24 hours. They also want Meta to explain how it ranks search results and produces answers with artificial intelligence. And they ask the court to enforce the daily fine of R$500,000 (about $99,000) it already set.

The new records involve searches for animated GIFs, the ordering of hashtags and answers from Meta AI, the artificial intelligence system built into WhatsApp. The organizations say the examples reinforce their suspicion that the platforms do not apply equivalent criteria to the two presidential campaigns.

Image searches put Flávio Bolsonaro in the spotlight

The petition describes a GIF search on WhatsApp for the word “brasil.” The first result was an image of Flávio Bolsonaro. It showed his ticket number and identified his running mate.

According to the records sent to the court, the same result appeared on three separate accounts. The groups use this to ask whether its top position comes from systematic ranking criteria.

A similar check on Instagram also showed images of the senator among the first results. Users who searched for “brasil” found three images of Flávio Bolsonaro in the top positions. The only mention of President Lula was his name in writing, with no photo.

The two organizations say the difference deserves an explanation. Search and recommendation tools can increase the exposure of certain candidates on social media. They are not claiming that they have proven bias in Meta, choosing instead to posit the question to the Superior Electoral Court.

Lula linked to derogatory content

Another set of examples ties Lula to negative terms in searches on Meta platforms.

On WhatsApp, a GIF search for the word “ladrão” (thief) returned a caricature of the president in a striped uniform, a reference to prison dress. Another result carried the message “Supporting the Workers’ Party is a mental illness.”

On Instagram, a search for the same word showed a GIF reading “Vote 13.” That is the Workers’ Party election number, tied to Lula’s candidacy.

For Sleeping Giants Brasil and CTRL+Z, these results point to an imbalance in how political references are shown to users. The imbalance stands out against the visibility of content favorable to Flávio Bolsonaro.

The petition also challenges how Instagram orders hashtags. A search for “lula” offered “#lulaladrão” (Lula thief) as the first suggestion, ahead of other terms about the president. A search for “bolsonaro” placed the critical hashtag “#bolsonaronuncamais” (Bolsonaro never again) among its last suggestions.

The groups cite the difference in position as another reason to investigate the relevance criteria the platform uses.

The issue is not only whether content for or against the candidates exists. It is mainly how automated systems organize that information and present it to the public.

Meta AI also questioned

The organizations included a test of Meta AI, the artificial intelligence tool offered to WhatsApp users. According to the petition, two people asked the system to pick a number between 1 and 25. They gave no instructions and made no reference to the election.

In one attempt, the AI answered 13. In the other, it answered 22. Those are the party ballot numbers of Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro, respectively.

The groups question the coincidence. They ask for an explanation of the parameters the system uses to form its answers.

The episode alone does not allow a conclusion that the tool answered out of electoral preference. Still, the organizations list the test among the elements that, in their view, demand more transparency about how the company’s artificial intelligence features work.

Electoral court demands compliance and threatens to double fine

The new records arrive as the electoral court takes a harder line with Meta.

Justice Bellizze had already ordered the company to apply identical criteria to the campaigns of Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro. He also ordered Meta to prove it was following the measures.

On Friday, the full court upheld the justice’s decision. It reinforced the company’s duty to ensure equal treatment of the candidates.

On Sunday, Bellizze again demanded action. He gave the company a new deadline of 24 hours to show it had met part of the court’s requirements.

The justice also warned that the daily fine, first set at R$500,000 (about $99,000), could rise to R$1 million (about $198,000) if noncompliance continues.

The new petition from Sleeping Giants Brasil and CTRL+Z aims to add to the case just as the court demands more detailed explanations from the company.

The groups want Meta to do more than fix the problems they identified. They also want it to disclose the criteria that decide the order of images, hashtag suggestions and answers produced by artificial intelligence.

Lula campaign has already gone to electoral court

The dispute began with complaints from Lula’s campaign about how Meta’s digital platforms work.

The president’s representatives pointed to limits on the circulation of content about his candidacy. They also cited differences in how the company’s tools behave compared with tools tied to his opponent.

The claims led the electoral court to demand measures to ensure equal treatment of the candidates.

Meta has denied deliberately favoring any candidate. It blamed the earlier problems on technical failures.

Folha de S.Paulo contacted the company about the new records filed Monday. Meta had not responded by the time of publication.

The lack of a specific response leaves open the explanations for the mechanisms behind the results the organizations found.

Groups call protest at Meta headquarters in São Paulo

Besides the legal action, Sleeping Giants Brasil and CTRL+Z planned a demonstration outside Meta’s headquarters in São Paulo at 5 p.m. Monday.

The event is called “Meta, Hands Off Our Election.” The organizations say it will be peaceful.

Participants plan to hand a notice to the company’s director in Brazil. They want action on the suspicions of unequal treatment of the candidacies.

The mobilization increases pressure on Meta on two fronts. In court, the groups seek correction of the alleged irregularities and sanctions. In public debate, they demand transparency about the algorithms used during the presidential race.

URL: https://github.com/slee-persis/GVS5H, See on Hacker News

GVS5H: Gorilla vs. 5 Humans

Results

Opus 5 ran on an earlier version of the scaffold, in a single pass served through OpenRouter rather than five on a pinned backend.

Abstract. Frontier coding performance is typically bought with larger proprietary models at high cost. We introduce ledger-based zero-shot self-orchestration, a training-free method in which fresh instances of one model decompose problems and coordinate through a shared filesystem holding a plan, notes and current solution. Across eleven open and closed-weight models on the 100 latest hard LiveCodeBench problems, the method yields gains of up to 25.6 percentage points on pinned backends and offers two routes to frontier-level accuracy. Orchestrated Qwen3.8 Flash Next reaches 93.0% pass@1 against Fable 5's 90.4% at 9% of the cost, and locally served, open-weight Qwen3.8-27B rises from 66.8% to 92.4%. Gains are not universal: some models are unchanged or worse. Transcript analysis attributes the gain to decomposition and persistent context. Inference-time organization can approach frontier coding accuracy at a fraction of the cost, or slightly exceed it on self-hostable weights.

— the paper

Running the code

Needs uv and an API key for the model you want to test.

cd codebase/v2-current
export OPENAI_API_KEY=...

ESCALATION_CLOUD_MAX_TOKENS=128000 \

Friday’s report came on the heels of a Brazilian court ruling on Thursday that ordered Meta to immediately adopt measures to provide equal treatment of the two candidates ahead of the runoff.

The ruling by a judge in Brazil’s top electoral court was made shortly after Lula filed a complaint that accused the tech giant – which owns Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp – of using biased algorithms and AI restrictions to favour opposition candidate Bolsonaro ahead of the election.

Justice Marco Aurelio Bellizze ruled that Meta cannot reduce the distribution of political content, restrict searches or remove posts in a way that creates an imbalance between Lula and Bolsonaro. His ruling also orders the company to ensure its artificial intelligence tool applies identical criteria to both candidacies.

Bellizze said in his ruling that Meta must pay a fine of 500,000 reais ($98,700) per day if it fails to comply.

According to Lula’s party, some of his posts appeared without a share button and had reduced reach. Options for reactions, sharing, audio or accelerated speed were also missing.

One of the most frequently asked questions we get is how we deploy large models on Cerebras wafer-scale chips. A single Cerebras WSE-3T wafer has 44 GB of on-chip memory, and trillion-parameter frontier models need terabytes for their weights alone.

In this post, we’ll explain how we split a large frontier model across multiple WSE-3T wafers, to run multi-trillion parameter models at 1000-2000+ tokens per second.

We’ll use the open source model Kimi K3, with ~3 trillion parameters, as an illustrative example.

By the end, you'll understand:

  • How we fit the full model into on-chip memory
  • How we map the model across multiple chips
  • How we handle a high # of concurrent requests

Breaking it down with Kimi K3

Kimi K3 is an open source, 3T parameter model with 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense layers.

For this illustrative example, we use:

  • A 256k assumed average request size
  • 4-bit weight quantization (like the Hugging Face implementation)
  • An 8-bit KV cache

#1: Size of Each layer

To calculate the total number of Cerebras WSE-3T wafers we need to support Kimi K3, let’s first calculate the size of each model layer.

#2: Number of Wafers

Now that we know each layer needs about 16 GB, we can figure out how many layers fit on each 44 GB wafer. The answer depends on the layer type:

  • Dense layers need additional room for a KV cache, because each dense (full-attention) layer stores the keys and values for every token in every active request. So, we place one dense layer per wafer and leave the remaining SRAM for its KV cache.
  • Linear-attention layers do not require additional room for a KV cache. Instead of storing keys and values for every token, a linear-attention layer keeps a small, fixed-size state per request, regardless of context length. That leaves room for two linear layers per wafer (2 × 16 GB = 32 GB).

This gives us a total wafer count of 35 + 24 = 59 wafers.

#3: Connecting the wafers together

Cerebras executes models in a pipeline. After the Cerebras compiler maps the model layers across regions of wafers, the runtime maps the path for tokens to flow between wafers. For ultrafast latency, only activations need to be passed between the wafers, and this can be done via RDMA over Ethernet. This is roughly 2 microseconds per hop.

It’s important to emphasize that because each Cerebras wafer has 44 GB of on-chip SRAM and each layer is only 16 GB, we are typically able to fit entire layers of the model directly on the chip.

This means that in most cases, the model weights never have to move, and layers don’t need to be split across wafers. Only activations cross from one wafer to the next.

#4: How we serve 1 request

Now that we have our wafers connected together and the model laid out, we can think of each wafer as one stage in an assembly line: the model’s weights for each stage stay in place, and the request’s intermediate results move through the layer stages.

For example, Wafer 1 runs model layers 1–2 and sends its activations to wafer 2. Wafer 2 runs layers 3–4 and passes its results to Wafer 3, and so on until the last wafer produces the next token.

#5: How we serve many requests

This raises a common misconception. If a token has to travel through each wafer in order, doesn’t each wafer sit idle while it waits for its turn? In effect, wouldn't the system be running at a batch size of one?

No! If we only sent one request down the line at a time and waited for it to complete before starting the next request, this would be an inefficient use of the pipeline. Instead, we keep the entire pipeline full with different requests. Because the model is split into pipeline stages already, each stage can work on a different request at the same time.

While stage 3 processes a token for request A, stage 2 processes one for request B, and stage 1 one for request C. In our example, each stage is a layer. In production, Cerebras uses much finer-grained stages, and many more of them.

Each stage can also process a micro-batch, a small group of requests, rather than a single request. So the number of requests in flight is roughly the number of stages times the micro-batch size.

To understand the tradeoff, smaller micro-batches make each request even faster, while larger micro-batches increase total throughput.

#6: How many requests can we serve?

The amount of on-chip memory allocated to KV cache determines the maximum number of concurrent requests. Every request in flight needs its own KV cache on each dense-layer wafer, so the size of on-chip memory sets the ceiling on concurrent requests. As explained above, we only need to calculate KV cache requirements for dense layers.

The total number of concurrent requests represents the number of simultaneous requests moving through the pipeline at any point in time. Unlike a GPU batch, those requests don’t wait for one another to finish, they stream through the pipeline continuously.

Of course, neither concurrency nor batch size tells you exactly how efficiently an inference system performs. When evaluating the throughput of an inference system, the more meaningful metric is total token throughput per unit of power (e.g. tokens per second per megawatt), when measured at the same output generation speed.

How this scales beyond 3T parameters

The same approach extends to larger models: calculate the memory needed for weights and request state, distribute the model across wafers, and connect them into a pipeline. Each additional wafer contributes compute and on-chip memory, allowing us to accommodate models that exceed the capacity of any single chip.

Entry 001 - Why gopher in 2026? May 22nd 2026 First off, if you're reading this, you're probably the kind of person who can't just use a tool, you have to know how it works. There are smart people who are good at what they do. Some people are master chefs, awesome mechanics, great sculptors or skillful accountants. But how many of those people dive so deep into what they are good at to understand what makes it tick? People like us are the ones who build a phlog for fun just to get a feeling for how far we've come with technology. Maybe you're here for the nostalgia, maybe it's to turn off the noise of modern tech. The important part is you are here now, in 2026 or beyond. I'm noticing a trend with my 17 year old and their friends with ADHD where they want to turn off the noise of the world and go back to simpler times. As one who is from those simpler times, I'm a little proud but also a little "Get off my lawn!" It's impossible to go back to that at this point and for better or worse, we have to make sense of where we are. Flip phones are simple and low- tech to them, but for us they were the latest in tech! We have syntax highlighting in vim that wasn't there when I was using vi so many years ago. Now I not only know it's there, but I can google how to set up so many features that I didn't know existed and would never figure out from the manual. Back in the day you had to find someone who first off knew what you were even talking about and second who knew more than you did. For me, this was how I ended up knowing a little about a lot but not being able to wrestle the arcane knowledge from the man pages. I think tech is in a weird place that is both super helpful and yet so unhelpful at the same time. item.title: America has lost 200k of jobs in media, film and the arts. How much is AI? (491 pts)

URL: https://www.apricitas.io/p/ai-and-the-fall-of-the-creative-class, See on Hacker News

Thanks for reading! If you haven’t subscribed, please click the button below:

By subscribing, you’ll join over 80,000 people who read Apricitas!

America has lost more than 200k jobs in “creative” industries over the last four years, with roughly 50k lost within the last year alone. That makes for one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history, with similar job loss intensity and duration occurring only during the major economic recessions of 2001 and 2008. Yet there’s no generalized recession today—instead, this period of job loss coincides with the rise of AI systems that can compose wholesale novels, photorealistic images, soundalike music, and practically every other form of digital art, en masse and at extremely low costs. Is this the fall of the Creative Class?

Proving the exact amount of AI-driven job loss in the arts is extremely difficult. Media firms are decidedly coy about their AI use, both to protect against public backlash and, more financially important, to preserve the legal basis for their copyrights. The effects of AI are also hard to disentangle from other factors currently affecting arts businesses, like consolidation in Hollywood, offshoring of content production, or the continued displacement of traditional media providers in favor of social media creators. Yet perhaps the clearest evidence of AI’s influence is just that all subsectors of the digital arts industry are losing jobs, while in-person entertainment is still growing at a healthy pace.

Some of those digital job losses are just a continuation of prior trends, like in the publishing industry where technological change has been continually grinding away newspaper and magazine jobs for decades. Yet for sectors like live broadcasting, streaming, or graphic design, recent experience is an unusual downturn compared to the tranquility of years prior. Then there’s the worst-hit sector, movie & sound recording, which has been bleeding jobs at a nearly unprecedented pace over the last three years.

Hollywood has never seen a stretch as bad as the last four years, with the movie & TV industry losing more than 100k jobs, nearly one-third of the sector’s total. At the depths touched this summer, total employment was lower than at any point since the 2008 recession and approaching the lowest point in 30 years. The streaming era has proven an extremely difficult transition, with traditional films and TV shows losing watch time to user-generated and increasingly AI-assisted or AI-generated content flows.

Overall, nearly half the media job losses of the last four years have been concentrated in the movie & sound recording sector that includes Hollywood. Written publishing has been the next-largest source of job loss, with employment down by more than 70k over the same time frame. Yet the job losses have by no means been contained to any particular part of media; instead they’ve hit nearly every subsector at some point. Nor do they show any sign of abating, with losses consistently hovering at around 50k per year and even accelerating in recent months. Will further AI development continue displacing workers in creative industries?

To understand what could happen to the business of art amidst the rise of AI, it’s important to understand what did happen to it during the first digital transition, the rise of the internet.

It was the turn of the millennium, and Metallica had a problem. Demos of their upcoming, unreleased tracks were bouncing around radio and the internet, originally leaked onto a new internet file-sharing website called Napster. There they found thousands of files shared amongst hundreds of thousands of users, many of which were direct rips of albums that sold for $15 being offered for free. The most anticipated albums were often leaked online even before they were on store shelves. Metallica sued Napster for copyright infringement, and they were soon joined by separate suits from other prominent artists and eventually the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA).

Much of the general public was understandably unsympathetic to Metallica, perceived as a bunch of already-successful millionaires trying to bilk even more money from listeners, and were even less sympathetic towards the RIAA, perceived as scurrilous middlemen who take from artists and fans alike. But the two of them easily won their lawsuit, forcing Napster into bankruptcy. Yet Metallica may have been right on the law but were on the wrong side of technology; the RIAA had won the battle but was losing the war.

The modern internet made file-sharing extremely easy, and no matter how much whac-a-mole companies played, they could not possibly catch every illegal upload. The perennial threat of piracy undermined their copyright and limited their ability to charge for music. Eventually, the value of individual songs fell to the point that companies like Spotify and Apple Music could swoop in to acquire massive catalogues, consolidate them, and charge a comparatively trivial fee for access. For what a single Metallica album would have cost in 2000, you can now get a month’s worth of unlimited access to nearly all human-made music.

The music industry has never returned to the heyday paydays of the peak CD era—even without adjusting for inflation, streaming revenue pales in comparison to ‘90s physical media sales. This was a massive boon to consumers, but it was also a squeeze on musicians that forced them to fundamentally change their business model over time. Instead of just selling records to earn money directly, music itself increasingly became a loss-leading advertisement for the live concerts (and merch) that provided a growing share of artists’ income. Tours got longer, venues got bigger, ticket prices skyrocketed, and musicians frequently took on roles closer to public influencers than isolated artistes. Were it not for rising concert sales, the business model of music would have completely collapsed, and the income going to musicians would have cratered.

Of course, there were still significant downsides to the transition into the streaming era. Bands (especially smaller ones) complain about the unending pressure to always be on tour. Musicians whose content was suited to home listening lost out to those more suited to giant festivals. Even accounting for concert revenues, musicians made less money than before. Yet musicians fared better than many areas of entertainment subsectors because there was a live component to fall back on—for many media industries, the digital era left no such comfort.

Over time, the business of video has moved in the opposite direction of music—out of the theatre and into the home. Hollywood formerly made most of its money enticing customers to visit sold-out movie theatres, but these were gradually supplanted by broadcast TV, cable, and physical media. Yet because each successful technological leap increased total video watch time, the industry was still able to thrive amidst technological upheaval. That is, until the modern streaming era.

Today, the plethora of video options and the rise of social media have sent video producers into a vicious competition for limited attention. Even before adjusting for inflation, movie ticket sales ended last year down 25% from their 2019 peak, cable revenue is down 18% from its peak, and streaming revenue has not been able to compensate for the drop. The mountain of free user-generated content on YouTube, Twitch, TikTok, or social media was already presenting harsh competition for traditional video companies in the years before ChatGPT’s launch, and now streaming services are also competing with a flood of AI-generated content. The business model of video media is fundamentally getting squeezed, and unlike in the music industry, there’s basically no equivalent to live concerts that Hollywood can be used to ease the pain.

The actual worst-case scenario for creative workers amidst the AI revolution is something similar to what happened to the publishing industry after the advent of the internet—that is, near-total collapse of their fundamental business model. Newspapers used to employ roughly half a million people in the US, more than the entire oil industry, and now their payrolls are down nearly 85% and still dropping. Magazine publishers likewise have let 66% of their staff go since the 90s, while book publishers have lost 40%.

The routine informational updates that previously formed newspapers’ bread-and-butter were all de-bundled—box scores moved to sports websites, stock movements went to financial websites, forecasts went to weather websites—each loss compounding on itself to undermine consumers’ need to buy the paper. Search engines became the first place people looked to for information, and newspapers’ advertising revenue rapidly started flowing to companies like Google instead. The collective of social media users became faster at breaking any news story than a daily paper could ever hope to be. When papers eventually did start aggressively paywalling content, the internet made it trivially easy for people to just copy the articles’ content and share it beyond the paywall. The entire business model had collapsed, to the point that now only a select few major newspapers can even survive.

That scale of copyright dilution and forced unbundling is the worst-case scenario for media businesses in the age of AI. It’s possible arts jobs could survive via consumers’ deep-seated aversion to explicitly AI-generated content, but AI is increasingly being used throughout media in ways invisible to the average end consumer. Roughly 32% of workers in the overall arts, entertainment, and recreation sector use Generative AI to some extent, which is less than the 62% average across all industries, but still enough that virtually every major media project could have some AI within its workflow.

Indeed, AI is likely seeping into media production processes in ways large companies themselves would struggle to prevent even when they desire to—how can a TV studio be sure nobody in their writers’ room is consulting ChatGPT for jokes or any storyboard artist is generating concept art? And even if professional TV and movie studios do effectively hold out against temptation and prevent internal AI use, how long can they compete with the large mass of wannabe independent creators with much fewer scruples? Plenty of media businesses tried to hold out against the algorithmic content waves of the 2010s and were buried as a result.

Yet fundamentally, it’s difficult to meaningfully predict how new technologies will interact with existing arts businesses. Take the unexpected resurgence in book sales over the last four years. The novel as a commercial art form had been struggling for decades, with fewer books sold in 2019 than at the beginning of the millennium, but the last six years have seen an unprecedented 70% surge in sales. The unlikely savior of the printed word came from perhaps its polar opposite—TikTok.

Of course, fewer people read now than ever before—for the general public, short-form video apps have accelerated the displacement of reading, just as TV, video games, or social media before them. Yet for a dwindling number of dedicated repeat readers, “BookTok” became a new way to source reviews, analysis, discourse, and community in a way that boosted the reading experience and absolutely turbocharged book sales. It’s possible that AI tools could have those same totally unpredictable spillovers for other museums, concerts, or other forms of art in ways that are unpredictable today, in much the same way short-form video saved books in ways that could never have been anticipated beforehand.

At the end of the day, the arts are only a small sector of the overall macroeconomy. Media made up a small share of the labor market even at its peak, and it has always been difficult to get hired in creative industries to the point that making fun of art students’ job prospects became an easy punchline. The movie industry has an income profile closer to eggs or bicycles than something major like healthcare or finance. Were the goal to create art for art’s sake, for the intangible and nonmonetizable cultural benefits, it would be relatively easy to counterbalance any economic impacts of AI on artists just by reversing recent cuts to the National Endowments for the Arts & Humanities.

It’s telling that Anthropic, the most prominent AI lab, has basically never bothered with image, video, or music generation, because the prospective economic benefits are marginal when compared to using AI to tackle math or scientific problems. OpenAI learned this lesson the hard way when it was forced to abandon its video generation platform Sora, deciding it had better use for its limited compute than making synthetic TikToks. Nowadays, the art generation is done primarily by secondary players running smaller models, though even these are large enough to threaten significant disruption to legacy media businesses.

In other words, the primary impacts of AI art will be on culture and society rather than the macroeconomy. Yet arts jobs might be a microcosm for other “creative-adjacent” work that occupies a much larger share of economic activity. Take the tech sector itself, which is the clearest place where AI-driven job loss has shown up outside the media business, as powerful coding agents replace human programmers. Annual tech job gains stood at nearly 300k in 2022, but the sector has been bleeding jobs every year since then in what is now its longest labor market downturn.

Right now, AI-driven job displacement has been relatively minor outside of these few narrow sectors. Unemployment is higher than it was four years ago but still below even the 2010s average, and overall job turnover rates remain extremely low. Some white-collar sectors that looked prime for AI automation have even been on a hiring spree over the last few years, including legal and engineering firms. Yet if the economic impact of AI ends up being anywhere near large enough to validate the trillions of dollars investors are currently betting on it, these economic disruptions will only spread from here.
